nodes.label: Pierre Bourdieu
nodes.date_label: Esquisse d’une théorie de la pratique (1972) · Outline of a Theory of Practice, translated by Richard Nice (1977) · La Distinction (1979) · Distinction, translated by Richard Nice (1984) · “L’illusion biographique” (1986)
nodes.description: Develops a relational account of social practice, taste and narrated lives. His habitus connects acquired dispositions with improvisation rather than reducing conduct to explicit rules or unconstrained choice. The selected Distinction conclusion examines classificatory struggles and social position; it does not certify one universal mechanism for all tastes. In “L’illusion biographique” he challenges retrospective stories that present a life as a naturally continuous project. Trajectories must be reconstructed across changing social fields, including the institutions and interview situations that help produce a named person’s apparent unity. The entry reuses precisely bounded earlier primary readings rather than claiming a new reading of the complete books.

nodes.label: Jürgen Habermas
nodes.date_label: Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit (1962) · “The Public Sphere”: original encyclopedia article (1964) · “The Public Sphere”: English translation (1974) · Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns (1981) · The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere: English translation (1989)
nodes.description: Distinguishes the public sphere of discussion from state authority and asks how communication can subject power to criticism. The encyclopedia article’s model of access is a normative problem rather than proof that historical bourgeois publics were inclusive. Its closing discussion leaves room for accountable organized communication rather than an inevitable narrative of complete decline. Nancy Fraser’s named 1990 criticism contests the bracketing of inequality and the assumption of one comprehensive public, while retaining the importance of publicity for democracy. The entry distinguishes this specifically attributed critique from a shared position of all feminist or gender historians.

nodes.label: Hannah Arendt
nodes.date_label: The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) · The Human Condition (1958) · Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) · Günter Gaus interview: politics and factual truth (1964)
nodes.description: Examines political action, public speech and the responsibility to preserve factual truth. In the selected 1964 Gaus interview she treats speaking and acting as ventures into relations with other people whose consequences cannot be predicted completely. Her defense of historical factual truth resists treating facts as mere opinion or allowing official rewriting to erase inconvenient persons and events. Her response to the Eichmann controversy is testimony from a participant in that controversy, not an independent verdict on every disputed judgment in the book. The profile distinguishes the primary interview selection from unread monographs and from the institutional bibliography that establishes their dates.

nodes.label: Judith Butler
nodes.date_label: “Performative Acts and Gender Constitution” (1988) · Gender Trouble (1990) · Bodies That Matter (1993)
nodes.description: Investigates the historically repeated acts through which gender becomes intelligible and is enforced. The selected 1988 essay treats embodiment as the taking up of possibilities constrained by inherited conventions, rather than an act by an already independent will. Its final pages ask how feminist representation can acknowledge diverse experiences without fixing women as a uniform natural category. The same argument questions a compulsory binary and heterosexual framework while recognizing punitive sanctions on departures from it. These particular primary pages supplement the earlier publisher-level Gender Trouble record; they do not establish a complete reading of that book or every later revision of performativity.

nodes.label: David Harvey
nodes.date_label: Social Justice and the City (1973) · The Condition of Postmodernity (1989) · “The Right to the City” (2008)
nodes.description: Connects urbanization and capitalist accumulation with questions of collective power over the city. The opening of his 2008 essay defines the right to the city as a collective capacity to reshape urbanization rather than merely individual access to existing resources. His selected 1989 discussion links place identity, tradition and flexible accumulation while allowing that regional resistance can have value without providing a sufficient programme of radical change. Doreen Massey’s named 1995 criticism contests that treatment of tradition and the possibilities of place. The entry presents a disputed spatial argument, rather than treating either position as a consensus of geographers or urban historians.

nodes.label: Maurice Halbwachs
nodes.date_label: La théorie de l’homme moyen (1912) · Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925) · La mémoire collective: posthumous publication (1950) · On Collective Memory: edited and translated selections (1992)
nodes.description: Studies remembering through social frameworks and the changing relations among groups. The selected French conclusion describes how families and religious communities revise their past as they encounter other groups and new present conditions; memory is neither an isolated mental archive nor a perfectly static inheritance. A separate statistical intervention examines the abstraction of an average human being. Canguilhem’s later discussion explicitly takes up that statistical criticism, a particular reception distinct from the collective-memory books. The English On Collective Memory is an edited and translated selection from earlier work, not the beginning of Halbwachs’s inquiry.

nodes.label: Mary Louise Pratt
nodes.date_label: “Arts of the Contact Zone” (1991) · Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation (1992) · Planetary Longings (2022)
nodes.description: Develops the contact zone as a way to examine encounters structured by unequal power. In the selected opening of “Arts of the Contact Zone,” colonial writing becomes a site of appropriation and response rather than an exchange between self-contained, homogeneous cultures. Her reading of Guaman Poma’s New Chronicle identifies autoethnography: subordinated subjects selectively use dominant genres and languages to address external representations and different audiences. This is Pratt’s particular reading of an Andean text; its historical details and contemporary Indigenous identities are not automatically certified by her theorization. The original article supplies the argument, while later book metadata supplies distinct publication facts.

nodes.label: Homi K. Bhabha
nodes.date_label: “Of Mimicry and Man: The Ambivalence of Colonial Discourse” (1984) · Nation and Narration: edited collection (1990) · The Location of Culture (1994) · Stierstorfer interview on diaspora and home (2013)
nodes.description: Examines cultural difference through contradiction, translation and the processes that produce minorities. In his interview with Klaus Stierstorfer, cultures do not form seamless wholes: their unequal, discordant relations help make theoretical problems visible. He distinguishes specific practices and trajectories from fixed cultural identity. His later discussion of home and refugee status resists treating all mobility as the same endless nomadism; choices, losses, legal positions and different time scales matter. These claims use his own interview answers rather than turning the earlier publisher description of hybridity and mimicry into a fresh chapter reading.
